title: Improper integrals
examples: How do I know if this integral has a real answer?
What is the difference between a normal integral and an improper one?
When do I need to use limits for integrals?

explain.say: Today we look at improper integrals which have infinite limits. These integrals are like normal ones but they go out to infinity.
When the limit of integration is infinity we must use a limit expression. We replace the infinity with a variable like t. Then we take the limit as t approaches infinity.
For example we evaluate the limit from a to t of x squared divided by t. Then we let t approach infinity.
Next we consider convergence. If the limit exists and is a finite number the integral converges. If the limit is infinity or does not exist it diverges.
Consider the integral from one to t of one divided by x squared. We take the limit as t approaches infinity. The result is one.

faq.q: What does it mean for an integral to converge?
faq.a: It means that the area under the curve approaches a specific, finite number. If it approaches infinity or nothing, it diverges.
asks: Does the area have a value?

faq.q: How do I handle the infinity limit?
faq.a: You replace the infinity symbol with a variable, say t. You then write the integral with t as the upper limit and take the limit as t approaches infinity.
asks: What do I do with infinity?
How do I set up the limit?

faq.a: No, not every improper integral converges. Some result in infinity or do not have a defined limit.
asks: Are there cases where it fails?

faq.q: What if the singularity is at the lower limit?
faq.a: If the function has a vertical asymptote at the lower limit, you treat it similarly. You replace the lower limit with a variable and take the limit as that variable approaches the problematic point.
asks: How do I handle division by zero?

faq.q: Is the integral of one over x always improper?
faq.a: No, it is only improper if the limits involve infinity or a point where the function is undefined. For example, from two to three it is normal.

facts: An improper integral occurs when one or both limits of integration are infinity.
When the limit is infinity, we use the definition of a limit to evaluate the integral.
If the limit exists and is a finite number, the integral converges.
If the limit is infinity or does not exist, the integral diverges.

quiz.why: The antiderivative of one over (t plus one) is the natural logarithm of (t plus one). Evaluating the limit gives the value one.

wrong.0: This confuses the function itself with the value of the definite integral.
wrong.2: This is tempting because the function approaches zero as t gets very large.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the limit actually settles on a specific finite number.

quiz.say: Does the integral \int{1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{x^2} dx converge or diverge?
quiz.why: The limit calculation results in a finite value, which confirms that the integral converges.

wrong.1: This is a common mistake when students see the function getting small.
wrong.2: The limit process provides a defined value, so it is not undefined.
wrong.3: While the value is one, the question asks about convergence, which is a true/false statement.

quiz.say: What is the value of \lim{t\to\infty} \int{2}^{t} \frac{1}{x} dx?
quiz.why: The natural logarithm function grows without bound as t approaches infinity, so the integral diverges.

wrong.1: This is the antiderivative, but the question asks for the limit value, not the function itself.
wrong.2: This only accounts for the lower limit and ignores the limit as t goes to infinity.
wrong.3: The integral does not approach zero; it grows without bound.
